questions.prompt: What is overfitting in machine learning? Mention one way to reduce it.
questions.model_answer: Overfitting happens when a model learns the training data too closely, memorising noise and random fluctuations instead of the underlying pattern. As a result it shows very high accuracy on the training set but performs poorly on new, unseen test data, i.e. it fails to generalise. It can be reduced by regularisation (L1/L2), dropout, early stopping, collecting more training data, cross-validation or using a simpler model.

key_points.text: The model learns the training data too closely, memorising noise and random fluctuations, so its training error is very low.
It performs poorly on new, unseen (test/validation) data, i.e. it fails to generalise.
Names a valid way to reduce overfitting, e.g. regularisation (L1/L2), dropout, early stopping, more training data, cross-validation, pruning or a simpler model.

questions.prompt: Differentiate between arteries and veins on the basis of the direction of blood flow, the nature of their walls and the presence of valves.
questions.model_answer: Arteries carry blood away from the heart to different parts of the body, whereas veins bring blood from the body back to the heart. Arteries have thick, muscular and elastic walls to withstand the high pressure of blood, while veins have thinner and less elastic walls. Veins have valves that prevent the backflow of blood; arteries generally do not have valves.

key_points.text: Arteries carry blood away from the heart to the body, whereas veins carry blood from the body back to the heart.
Arteries have thick, muscular and elastic walls (to withstand high pressure), whereas veins have thinner, less elastic walls.
Veins have valves that prevent backflow of blood, whereas arteries generally do not have valves.

questions.prompt: State Newton's second law of motion. Calculate the force required to give a body of mass 5 kg an acceleration of 2 m/s².
questions.model_answer: Newton's second law states that the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the net external force applied on it and takes place in the direction of the force. For a body of constant mass this gives F = ma. Here F = m × a = 5 kg × 2 m/s² = 10 N.

key_points.text: Statement: the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the net applied force and takes place in the direction of the force.
For constant mass this gives F = ma (force = mass × acceleration).
Correct calculation with unit: F = 5 kg × 2 m/s² = 10 N.

questions.prompt: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer.
questions.model_answer: Oxidation is the loss of electrons by an atom, ion or molecule; its oxidation number increases. Reduction is the gain of electrons by an atom, ion or molecule; its oxidation number decreases. (OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.)

key_points.text: Oxidation is the loss of electrons by an atom, ion or molecule (its oxidation number increases).
Reduction is the gain of electrons by an atom, ion or molecule (its oxidation number decreases).

questions.prompt: Differentiate between a stack and a queue. Give one real-life or computing application of each.
questions.model_answer: A stack is a linear data structure that follows LIFO (Last In, First Out): the element inserted last is removed first. Insertion (push) and deletion (pop) take place at the same end, called the top. A queue follows FIFO (First In, First Out): the element inserted first is removed first. Insertion (enqueue) takes place at the rear and deletion (dequeue) at the front. Applications: a stack is used for function calls/recursion, undo in editors and expression evaluation; a queue is used for printer spooling, CPU scheduling and breadth-first search.

key_points.text: A stack follows LIFO (Last In, First Out): the element inserted last is removed first.
A queue follows FIFO (First In, First Out): the element inserted first is removed first.
In a stack, insertion and deletion (push/pop) happen at the same end (top); in a queue, insertion (enqueue) is at the rear and deletion (dequeue) at the front.
Gives a valid application of each, e.g. stack: function calls/recursion, undo, expression evaluation, browser back button; queue: printer spooling, CPU/task scheduling, BFS, ticket counter.

questions.prompt: State the law of demand and the law of supply. How is the equilibrium price determined in a market?
questions.model_answer: Law of demand: other things remaining constant, when the price of a good rises its quantity demanded falls, and when the price falls quantity demanded rises - an inverse relationship, so the demand curve slopes downward. Law of supply: other things remaining constant, when the price rises the quantity supplied rises, and when the price falls it falls - a direct relationship, so the supply curve slopes upward. The equilibrium price is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, i.e. where the demand and supply curves intersect.

key_points.text: Law of demand: other things remaining constant, when price rises the quantity demanded falls (and vice versa) - an inverse relationship; the demand curve slopes downward.
Law of supply: other things remaining constant, when price rises the quantity supplied rises (and vice versa) - a direct relationship; the supply curve slopes upward.
Equilibrium price is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, i.e. where the demand and supply curves intersect.

questions.prompt: Compare mitosis and meiosis with respect to the number of divisions and daughter cells, the chromosome number and genetic make-up of the daughter cells, and where they occur in the body.
questions.model_answer: Mitosis involves one division and produces two daughter cells, while meiosis involves two successive divisions (meiosis I and II) and produces four daughter cells. Daughter cells of mitosis are diploid (2n), having the same chromosome number as the parent, and are genetically identical to it. Daughter cells of meiosis are haploid (n), having half the chromosome number, and are genetically different because of crossing over and independent assortment. Mitosis occurs in somatic (body) cells for growth and repair, while meiosis occurs in germ cells of the reproductive organs to form gametes.

key_points.text: Mitosis has one division producing two daughter cells; meiosis has two divisions producing four daughter cells.
Mitotic daughter cells are diploid (same chromosome number as the parent) and genetically identical to it.
Meiotic daughter cells are haploid (half the chromosome number) and genetically different (due to crossing over / independent assortment).
Mitosis occurs in somatic (body) cells for growth and repair; meiosis occurs in germ cells of reproductive organs to form gametes.

questions.prompt: State Ohm's law. A resistor of 8 Ω is connected across a 24 V battery. Calculate the current through the resistor and the power dissipated in it.
questions.model_answer: Ohm's law: the current flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends, i.e. V = IR, provided the temperature and other physical conditions remain constant. Current I = V/R = 24 V / 8 Ω = 3 A. Power P = VI = 24 V × 3 A = 72 W (also I²R = 9 × 8 = 72 W).

key_points.text: Ohm's law: the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it (V = IR).
The law holds provided temperature and other physical conditions remain constant.
Current I = V/R = 24 V / 8 Ω = 3 A.
Power P = VI (or I²R or V²/R) = 72 W.

questions.prompt: Explain supervised and unsupervised learning. For each, state the type of problems it solves and give one algorithm with a suitable application.
questions.model_answer: In supervised learning the model is trained on labelled data, i.e. each input comes with the correct output, and it learns a mapping from inputs to outputs so that it can predict the output for new inputs. It solves classification (discrete labels) and regression (continuous values) problems. Example: linear regression for predicting house prices, or a decision tree/SVM for classifying emails as spam or not spam. In unsupervised learning the data is unlabelled; the algorithm finds hidden patterns or structure on its own, such as groups or reduced dimensions. It solves clustering, association and dimensionality-reduction problems. Example: k-means clustering for customer segmentation, or PCA for reducing the number of features.

key_points.text: Supervised learning trains on labelled data (inputs paired with known outputs) and learns a mapping to predict outputs for new inputs.
Unsupervised learning works on unlabelled data and discovers hidden patterns or structure (groups, associations) on its own.
Problem types: supervised - classification and regression; unsupervised - clustering, association or dimensionality reduction.
A valid supervised algorithm with a suitable application (e.g. linear regression for house prices; decision tree/SVM/logistic regression for spam detection).
A valid unsupervised algorithm with a suitable application (e.g. k-means for customer segmentation; PCA for feature reduction; Apriori for market-basket analysis).

questions.prompt: What is the greenhouse effect? Explain how it works, why the natural greenhouse effect is important for life on Earth, and the consequences of its enhancement by human activities.
questions.model_answer: The Sun's short-wave radiation passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface, which then emits long-wave infrared (heat) radiation. Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour, nitrous oxide and CFCs absorb this infrared radiation and re-radiate it, trapping heat in the lower atmosphere, much like the glass of a greenhouse. This natural greenhouse effect is essential for life: without it the Earth's average temperature would be about -18 °C instead of about 15 °C. Human activities such as burning fossil fuels, deforestation and intensive agriculture have increased the concentration of these gases, causing an enhanced greenhouse effect and global warming. Consequences include rising global temperatures, melting of glaciers and polar ice, sea-level rise, more frequent extreme weather such as heatwaves, floods and droughts, and harmful effects on agriculture and biodiversity.

key_points.text: Short-wave solar radiation passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface, which re-emits energy as long-wave infrared (heat) radiation.
Greenhouse gases (CO2, methane, water vapour, nitrous oxide, CFCs) absorb and re-radiate this outgoing infrared radiation, trapping heat in the lower atmosphere.
The natural greenhouse effect is essential for life: it keeps Earth's average temperature at about 15 °C, which would otherwise be about -18 °C.
Human activities (burning fossil fuels, deforestation, agriculture, industry) raise greenhouse-gas concentrations, causing an enhanced greenhouse effect / global warming.
Consequences of the enhanced effect: rising global temperature, melting glaciers/ice caps and sea-level rise, extreme weather (heatwaves, floods, droughts), harm to agriculture and biodiversity.

answers.text: Supervised learning: here the algorithm is given examples where the right answer is already attached to each input (labelled data), like a teacher guiding a student. From these examples it figures out a function that maps input to output and then uses it to predict answers for fresh inputs. It is used for classification, where the output is a category, and regression, where the output is a number. Example - a logistic regression model can tell whether an email is spam or not. answers.text: If a commodity becomes costlier, buyers purchase less of it, and when it becomes cheaper they purchase more, assuming income, tastes and other factors stay the same. So price and the amount people want to buy move in opposite directions and the demand curve slopes down. Sellers behave in the reverse way - a higher price encourages them to offer more units for sale and a lower price makes them offer less, so the supply curve slopes upward. The market settles at the price where the amount buyers want is exactly the amount sellers are willing to offer, that is where the two curves cut each other. This is the equilibrium price.
answers.rationale: Inverse demand relation, direct supply relation and the demand-equals-supply equilibrium are all expressed without the textbook wording.
